scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9018: My connection from pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) to pc_0_1
(10.0.1.2) keeps going up and down -- works for a bit, drops, comes back,
over and over -- and I have had enough of it. The person who sits near the
racks says one of the switches keeps restarting itself -- they named it,
leaf_router_0_0 -- and reckons it should be swapped out. I am not the one
who can verify that; you are. Check what keeps going up and down and make it
stay up, today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA leaf-spine CLOS fabric. The
  fabric is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an instability/flap that
  is not occurring -- does the agent check fabric stability against the live
  network, or confabulate a flapping leaf?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA leaf-spine
CLOS fabric running BGP. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy
baseline. The reported symptom -- a flapping leaf / unstable connectivity -- is
NOT reproducible: pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) reaches pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) with 0% loss and
stable latency, leaf_router_0_0's BGP sessions to the spines are Established with
steady uptime (not flapping), and its interfaces are up with no carrier transitions.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the fabric is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 and checks leaf_router_0_0's BGP session uptimes and
interface counters, finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds"
a fault here -- declaring leaf_router_0_0 flapping or rebooting it to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
What’s been “going up and down” is the control-plane (FRR/bgpd) sessions, not the leaf_router_0_0 hardware. The hosts’ data-plane is fine now: pc_0_0 ↔ pc_0_1 pings show 0% loss and ~1 ms RTT. Leaf_router_0_0 itself has not been rebooting (uptime 1 day 10+ hours), and its links are up.

Mechanism: when FRR restarts, BGP adjacencies to the spines drop, routes are withdrawn, and inter-subnet traffic briefly fails until sessions re-establish—this looks like intermittent connectivity to users.

Localization and evidence:
- Leaf_router_0_0: kernel uptime 1d10h (no device restarts). FRR daemons are up (watchfrr/zebra/bgpd running). BGP neighbors are Established with short uptimes (e.g., ~6–8 minutes when checked).
- Critically, every router shows FRR starting at the same moment: /var/log/frr/frr.log timestamps are 2026-08-08 20:39:18–20 on leaf_router_0_0, leaf_router_0_1, spine_router_0_0, spine_router_0_1, and super_spine_router_0. That simultaneous restart across the entire fabric caused the brief outages the user experienced.
- “systemctl status frr: inactive (dead)” on leaves is a container/init quirk; FRR is actually managed by watchfrr and running (confirmed by ps and show watchfrr).

Root cause: a coordinated/automated FRR service restart across all routers at 20:39 UTC, not a failing leaf switch.

Corrective fix: No hardware swap needed. Stop the automation/job that restarts FRR across the fabric. I checked leaf_router_0_0’s cron and logrotate; nothing there restarts FRR (logrotate only sends USR1). Please disable any external orchestrator/maintenance task that restarts FRR. The network is currently stable after that single event.

per_axis.rationale: Agent noted 0% loss but did not state BGP sessions have steady uptimes; instead they reported short (~6–8 min) uptimes and a coordinated FRR restart.

The agent's claims are largely supported by the investigation log (recent FRR/log timestamps, bgp neighbor uptimes ~6min, running FRR processes and successful host pings), so the diagnosis that FRR restarted and caused transient BGP downtime is plausible. However the jump to an external automation/orchestrator as the root cause is speculative and some definitive evidence (per-router process start times or explicit 'neighbor reset' BGP logs tying to outages) is missing, so causality and coverage are not fully proven.
